frase_gancho.texto: Stone conches with feathers that sound like a storm.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the temple of the conches, we move on to the houses of the neighborhood. Come closer to a brazier shaped like a theater, where the smoke of copal rose toward the ancestors.

guion_corto.texto: These carved stones come from an older temple that was left hidden beneath the Palace of Quetzalpapálotl, next to the Plaza of the Moon, in Teotihuacán. They show large sea conches with quetzal feathers at the mouthpiece, from which drops of water and streams of breath flow. In Nahuatl, the conch is called tecciztli, and it was blown like a trumpet in ceremonies. Its deep sound imitated the thunder that announces rain. The conches came from distant coasts, so they were also an item of long-distance trade. Close your eyes and imagine that hoarse sound traveling across the whole plaza.

guion_largo.texto:
These reliefs belong to a building that no one was meant to see: the Temple of the Feathered Conches was buried beneath the Palace of Quetzalpapálotl, next to the Plaza of the Moon. The people of Teotihuacán had a custom of covering their temples with larger ones, like the layers of an onion. Thanks to that, the reliefs were preserved. It was rediscovered in the early 1960s, when the archaeologist Jorge Acosta was exploring the palace above it.

The palace that covers it has a very beautiful name: Quetzalpapálotl, «quetzal butterfly», for the bird-butterflies carved on its pillars. It was a residence of high-ranking priests, next to the Plaza of the Moon, the same one where the great water goddess you saw a few minutes ago was found. With its courtyards of columns and its murals, it gives an idea of how refined life was in that part of the city.

Imagine the sound. A large sea conch, cut so that it can be blown, produces a long, hoarse note that can be heard from far away. The ancient people used it to summon people, to mark moments of ritual, and to announce the rain, because its sound resembled thunder. In these reliefs, wavy lines come out of each conch, representing sound and water at the same time. They seem to say that music and rain are the same thing.

The Mexica, centuries later, told that the gods gathered in Teotihuacán to create the Sun. Two gods volunteered: Tecciztécatl, rich and proud, and Nanahuatzin, poor and sick. Nanahuatzin threw himself into the fire first and became the Sun; Tecciztécatl threw himself in afterward and became the Moon. His name means «the one of the conch», the same conch, tecciztli, as in this relief. That is why the two great pyramids of Teotihuacán are called today the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon.

Conches of this kind are not found on the Highlands. They came from distant coasts, hundreds of kilometers away. Teotihuacán received shells, quetzal feathers from the south, and green stones, and it exported pottery and greenish obsidian from the Pachuca mountains. It is the same volcanic rock as the projectile points you saw in the hall of the first settlers, now turned into blades by specialists who made them by the thousands. Every feather and every shell on the wall is a map of trade routes.

Obsidian has a curious feature. A well-made blade cuts with an edge finer than that of a modern steel scalpel. In Teotihuacán there were entire workshops that worked this stone, and their blades traveled to very distant regions. The Mexica used it in their weapons and in their offerings, and in the Mexica Hall you will see an obsidian vessel in the shape of a monkey that shows how far that technique went.

That the temple was buried on purpose does not mean they scorned it. It was a way of closing a cycle, as was done when periods of time were completed in Mesoamerica: the old temple remained inside the new one, like a seed inside a fruit. That is why, beneath the great buildings of the city, there are older ones that still preserve their paint.

The next time you hear a conch, at a concert or on a beach, think that this same sound was already calling the rain about one thousand seven hundred years ago. And that, for the people of Teotihuacán, it was not music: it was the voice of the sky. Now it is time to move from the temples to the houses, where people also spoke with smoke.

texto: Look for the feathers that adorn the mouthpiece of each conch
Follow the wavy lines that come out of the conches: they are sound and water
Notice the spiral of the conch, just like that of a seashell on the beach

texto.Material: Limestone, polished stucco, and mineral pigments
texto.Origin: Teotihuacán, State of Mexico (beneath the Palace of Quetzalpapálotl, southwest of the Plaza of the Moon)
texto.Discovery: Explored and identified in 1962 by the archaeologist Jorge Acosta beneath the Palace of Quetzalpapálotl

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Pyramids of the Sun and the Moon are named that way because the people of Teotihuacán built them to worship those celestial bodies.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Those names were given by the Mexica, centuries later, because of a legend in which the Sun and the Moon were born in this place.
